title: Marguerite and the Confession
premise: Orsen Coldharbour, an estate lawyer with a flawless record of closing cases, is hired to probate a will for Marguerite Vane, a woman who vanished thirty years ago and was declared dead in absentia. The will's existence is impossible — dated after her disappearance — and when Orsen finds her diary, the entries continue past the date she vanished, written in ink that hasn't dried. As the statute of limitations on the crimes surrounding her disappearance expires in ninety days, Orsen must unravel alibis woven three decades ago by the estate's beneficiaries, discovering that Marguerite staged her own vanishing to expose a death she witnessed — and that someone has been maintaining her diary ever since to keep watch. In the end, Orsen finds Marguerite alive under a new identity, but exposing the truth means destroying the innocent daughter who inherited everything; Orsen chooses justice outside the law, sealing the confession inside the will itself, readable only after every beneficiary dies.
about_author: Ulyana Coldharbour is the pseudonym of a former probate clerk who spent eleven years cataloguing the unclaimed estates of the wealthy. They write mysteries from a converted tithe barn on the Yorkshire moors, where they claim every will tells a lie if you read it closely enough.

chapters.title: The Will That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. A courier delivers a sealed will for Marguerite Vane, missing thirty years and legally dead. The document is dated four years after her disappearance, notarized by a stamp office that closed in 1994. Orsen's pride in never refusing a case wars with professional instinct screaming fraud. Emotional beat: cold fascination masking unease.

chapters.title: Vane House
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Orsen travels to the decaying Vane estate to meet the beneficiaries: Marguerite's brother Aldous, her former business partner Cressida Hale, and her estranged daughter Imogen, who was six when her mother vanished. Each greets the will with a different mask — contempt, fear, hope. Emotional beat: the house itself feels like a witness.

chapters.title: Terms of Probate
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. The will's terms are strange: the estate passes to Imogen only if Orsen closes 'the question of my death' within ninety days, before the statute expires. Failure voids everything. Aldous objects loudly; Cressida goes pale. Orsen accepts, unable to resist the puzzle. Emotional beat: ambition overriding caution.

chapters.title: The Diary
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Searching Marguerite's locked study, Orsen finds a diary whose final entry is dated the day she disappeared — then keeps going, another decade of entries in the same handwriting. The last line reads: 'If you are reading this, you are already inside it.' Emotional beat: vertigo, the case turning personal.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Alibi
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Orsen reconstructs the night of the disappearance from old police files: all three beneficiaries have airtight alibis, corroborated down to the minute — too perfect, as if rehearsed. The investigating officer, DS Renwick, retired rather than close the file. Emotional beat: suspicion crystallizing into method.

chapters.title: Imogen
chapters.summary: POV: Imogen. Imogen remembers almost nothing of her mother except a lullaby sung in a voice that wasn't hers. She confesses to Orsen that she received a birthday card every year until she turned eighteen, unsigned, postmarked nowhere. Emotional beat: grief she never got to finish feeling.

chapters.title: Renwick's Regret
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Orsen tracks down DS Renwick, now dying in a coastal cottage. He admits he was pressured to accept the alibis by someone above him, and gives Orsen a name half-burned from an old notebook: 'C— H——' and one word, 'witness.' Emotional beat: a dying man handing over his shame.

chapters.title: Cressida's Ledger
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Digging into Cressida Hale's finances, Orsen finds annual payments for thirty years to an account labeled only 'M.V. — maintenance.' Someone has been paying to keep something — or someone — quiet. Emotional beat: the thrill of the first real crack.

chapters.title: What the Diary Knows
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Reading the post-disappearance entries closely, Orsen realizes they describe events after March 1994 with impossible accuracy — including a fire at Vane House that killed a groundskeeper. The diary isn't a record; it's surveillance. Emotional beat: dread replacing curiosity.

chapters.title: Aldous Breaks
chapters.summary: POV: Aldous. Cornered by Orsen about the payments, Aldous admits he knew Marguerite planned to disappear — she told him she'd seen something she couldn't survive reporting through legal channels. He swore silence to protect Imogen. Emotional beat: loyalty as both shield and cage.

chapters.title: The Groundskeeper's Fire
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Orsen reopens the 1996 fire: ruled accidental, but the victim, Tomas Bell, had recently been hired — and his employment contract bears Marguerite's signature, dated after her disappearance. Someone with access to her identity was operating openly. Emotional beat: the past pressing into the present.

chapters.title: Someone Is Watching
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Orsen's hotel room is searched; pages of the diary photocopies are taken. A note left behind reads: 'Stop before the statute does.' Orsen realizes the diary's keeper knows exactly where they are. Emotional beat: hunter becoming hunted.

chapters.title: Cressida Confesses Everything Except the Truth
chapters.summary: POV: Cressida. Cressida admits to paying 'maintenance' — but claims it was blackmail: someone with Marguerite's handwriting has extorted her since 1995. She shows Orsen twenty years of demands. If Marguerite is dead, who writes like her? Emotional beat: terror wearing composure.

chapters.title: Handwriting
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. A forensic graphologist confirms the diary entries and the blackmail letters share authorship — and match Marguerite's hand beyond forgery probability. Either she lives, or someone learned to write as her over decades. Orsen begins to suspect which. Emotional beat: the ground shifting beneath certainty.

chapters.title: Imogen's Card
chapters.summary: POV: Imogen. Imogen brings Orsen her final birthday card, age eighteen. Hidden in the paper stock is a watermark: a lighthouse matching one on the Cornish coast from a photograph in Marguerite's study. She asks Orsen, quietly, whether finding the truth will cost her the mother-shaped hole she's built her life around. Emotional beat: love versus truth made flesh.

chapters.title: Ninety Days Become Nine
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. With the statute days from expiring, Orsen follows the watermark to Cornwall and finds a cottage registered under an alias used by Tomas Bell. Inside: decades of diaries, all in Marguerite's hand, and a fresh cup of tea still warm. Emotional beat: breathless pursuit.

chapters.title: Marguerite
chapters.summary: POV: Marguerite. Marguerite Vane returns to her own cottage and finds Orsen waiting. She doesn't run. She explains: she witnessed Cressida murder her business partner in 1994, knew the alibis were untouchable, and chose vanishing — becoming the witness no one could kill because no one knew she existed. Emotional beat: relief and fury in equal measure.

chapters.title: The Keeper of the Diary
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. But Marguerite didn't write the later entries — Tomas Bell did, her ally, keeping the surveillance alive until the fire meant to kill him. His death broke her pact of patience. The recent escalation, the note to Orsen, came from her: the statute's expiry is her deadline for revenge. Emotional beat: sympathy curdling into alarm.

chapters.title: Confession at Vane House
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Orsen brings Marguerite to Vane House where Cressida, tipped off, waits with Aldous and Imogen. Confrontation detonates: Cressida confesses to the 1994 killing believing Marguerite already dead and the statute nearly run. But Orsen recorded it — and the statute covers concealment, a charge still live. Emotional beat: the climax, truth tearing the room open.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Cressida's arrest unravels the old alibis; Renwick's pressure is traced to her late husband, a magistrate. But Marguerite faces charges too — false identity, extortion. Orsen offers her the lawyer's last trick: the will's contingency clause lets her legally remain dead if the 'question' is closed ambiguously. Emotional beat: Orsen choosing mercy over the clean win.

chapters.title: The Question of My Death
chapters.summary: POV: Imogen. Imogen learns her mother is alive and chooses not to see her — some absences can't be repaired, only honored. She inherits the estate and burns nothing, changes nothing, keeping the study locked. Emotional beat: grief finally given its true shape.

chapters.title: Closing the File
chapters.summary: POV: Orsen. Orsen seals the case: the will probated, the question marked 'resolved,' Marguerite gone again by dawn — this time by choice, leaving Orsen the diary's final volume with a single new entry thanking them. Orsen takes no new cases for a month, then accepts one, because a closed question is just an opening. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace.
